"'''Oh, Pretty Woman'''" (or simply "'''Pretty Woman'''") is a song recorded by [[Roy Orbison]] and written by Orbison and [[Bill Dees]].<ref name="500 Number One Hits">{{cite book| first= Jo| last= Rice|year= 1982| title= The Guinness Book of 500 Number One Hits| edition= 1st| publisher= Guinness Superlatives Ltd | location= Enfield, Middlesex| page= 85| isbn= 0-85112-250-7}}</ref> It was released as a single in August 1964 on [[Monument Records]] and spent three weeks at number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] from September 26, 1964, making it the second and final single by Orbison (after "[[Running Scared (Roy Orbison song)|Running Scared]]") to reach number one in the United States.<ref>[[Fred Bronson|Bronson, Fred]] (2003). ''The Billboard Book of #1 Hits'', 5th Edition (Billboard Publications), page 157.</ref> It was also Orbison's third single to top the [[UK singles chart|UK Singles Chart]], where it spent three weeks at number one.<ref name="British Hit Singles & Albums">{{cite book| first= David| last= Roberts| year= 2006| title= [[British Hit Singles & Albums]]| edition= 19th| publisher= Guinness World Records Limited | location= London| isbn= 1-904994-10-5| page= 186}}</ref>

The single version (in mono) and the LP version (in stereo on the [[Orbisongs|Orbisongs LP]]) have slightly differing lyrics. The LP version with the intended lyric: "come ''with'' me baby" was changed for the single to "come '''to''' me baby" as the former was considered too risque. The record ultimately sold seven million copies and marked the high point in Orbison's career.<ref>Lehman, Peter. ''Roy Orbison: Invention of an Alternative Rock Masculinity''. Philadelphia: Temple UP, 2003, p. 2, 13</ref> In October 1964, the single was certified [[gold record|gold]] by the [[Recording Industry Association of America|RIAA]].<ref>{{cite certification|region=United States|title=Pretty Woman|artist=Roy Orbison}}</ref> At the year's end, ''Billboard'' ranked it the [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1964|number four song of 1964]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|date=January 2, 1965|title=Hot 100 Singles of 1964|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1965/Billboard%201965-01-02.pdf|magazine=Billboard}}</ref>

"Oh, Pretty Woman" was later used for the title of the 1990 film ''[[Pretty Woman]]'' and its 2018 [[Pretty Woman (musical)|Broadway musical adaptation]]. [[Acuff-Rose Music]]'s lawsuit over a [[parody]] of "Oh, Pretty Woman" by [[2 Live Crew]] led to a [[U.S. Supreme Court]] ruling (''[[Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.]]'') establishing that parody was a valid form of [[fair use]].<ref name=":1" />

"Oh, Pretty Woman" (or simply "Pretty Woman") is a song recorded by Roy Orbison and written by Orbison and Bill Dees. It was released as a single in August 1964 on Monument Records and spent three weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 from September 26, 1964, making it the second and final single by Orbison (after "Running Scared") to reach number one in the United States. It was also Orbison's third single to top the UK Singles Chart, where it spent three weeks at number one.

The single version (in mono) and the LP version (in stereo on the Orbisongs LP) have slightly differing lyrics. The LP version with the intended lyric: "come with me baby" was changed for the single to "come to me baby" as the former was considered too risque. The record ultimately sold seven million copies and marked the high point in Orbison's career. In October 1964, the single was certified gold by the RIAA. At the year's end, Billboard ranked it the number four song of 1964.

"Oh, Pretty Woman" was later used for the title of the 1990 film Pretty Woman and its 2018 Broadway musical adaptation. Acuff-Rose Music's lawsuit over a parody of "Oh, Pretty Woman" by 2 Live Crew led to a U.S. Supreme Court ruling (Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.) establishing that parody was a valid form of fair use.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.wikitext:
The title was inspired by Orbison's wife, Claudette, interrupting a conversation to announce that she was going out. When Orbison asked if she had enough cash, his co-writer Bill Dees interjected, "A pretty woman never needs any money."<ref>Amburn, Ellis. ''Dark Star: The Roy Orbison Story''. New York: Carol Publishing, 1995, p. 127</ref>

Orbison's recording of the song was produced by [[Fred Foster]]<ref name="500 Number One Hits" /> and engineered by [[Bill Porter (sound engineer)|Bill Porter]]<ref>{{Cite AV media notes |title=The Monument Story |others=Various |publisher=Sony Music Entertainment |id=A2K66106 |location=New York, New York}}</ref> on August 1, 1964. There were four guitar players at the session: Orbison, Billy Sanford, [[Jerry Kennedy]], and [[Wayne Moss]].<ref name=SessionReport>{{citation |date=7 September 1964 |title=Phonograph Recording Contract, Local Union No. 257 |publisher=American Federation of Musicians of the United States and Canada |location=Fred Foster Sound Studios, Nashville, TN}}</ref> Sanford, who later played on sessions for [[Elvis Presley]], [[Don Williams]], and many others, played the song's introductory guitar [[riff]]. Other musicians on the recording included [[Floyd Cramer]] on piano, [[Henry Strzelecki]] on bass, [[Boots Randolph]] and [[Charlie McCoy]] on saxophones, [[Buddy Harman]] on drums, and Paul Garrison on percussion.<ref name=SessionReport /> Dees sang harmony vocals, as he did on many Orbison songs.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.songfacts.com/facts/roy-orbison/its-over |title=It's Over by Roy Orbison |access-date=2022-09-01 |website=Songfacts}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=March 2025}} ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' described the song as having a "great dance beat coupled with fine arrangement."<ref name=bb>{{cite news|newspaper=Billboard|access-date=2021-04-04|date=August 15, 1964|page=12|title=Singles Reviews|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1964/Billboard%201964-08-15.pdf}}</ref> ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' described it as "a catchy, quick-beat salute with a number of ear-catching rockin' ingredients."<ref name=cb>{{cite magazine |title=CashBox Record Reviews |date=August 22, 1964 |page=12 |access-date=2022-01-12 |url=https://worldradiohstory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/60s/1964/CB-1964-08-22.pdf |magazine=Cash Box}}{{dead link|date=May 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

Orbison posthumously won the 1991 [[Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance]] for the recording of "Oh, Pretty Woman" from his 1988 [[HBO]] television special ''[[Roy Orbison and Friends: A Black and White Night]]''. In 1999, the song was inducted into the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]] and was named one of the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]'s [[The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll|500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll]]. In 2004, ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' magazine ranked the song at number 224 on their "[[500 Greatest Songs of All Time]]" list. On May 14, 2008, the [[Library of Congress]] selected the song for preservation in the [[National Recording Registry]].
sections.text:
The title was inspired by Orbison's wife, Claudette, interrupting a conversation to announce that she was going out. When Orbison asked if she had enough cash, his co-writer Bill Dees interjected, "A pretty woman never needs any money."

Orbison's recording of the song was produced by Fred Foster and engineered by Bill Porter on August 1, 1964. There were four guitar players at the session: Orbison, Billy Sanford, Jerry Kennedy, and Wayne Moss. Sanford, who later played on sessions for Elvis Presley, Don Williams, and many others, played the song's introductory guitar riff. Other musicians on the recording included Floyd Cramer on piano, Henry Strzelecki on bass, Boots Randolph and Charlie McCoy on saxophones, Buddy Harman on drums, and Paul Garrison on percussion. Dees sang harmony vocals, as he did on many Orbison songs.{{better source needed|date=March 2025}} Billboard described the song as having a "great dance beat coupled with fine arrangement." Cash Box described it as "a catchy, quick-beat salute with a number of ear-catching rockin' ingredients."

Orbison posthumously won the 1991 Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance for the recording of "Oh, Pretty Woman" from his 1988 HBO television special Roy Orbison and Friends: A Black and White Night. In 1999, the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame and was named one of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll. In 2004, Rolling Stone magazine ranked the song at number 224 on their "500 Greatest Songs of All Time" list. On May 14, 2008, the Library of Congress selected the song for preservation in the National Recording Registry.

sections.heading: Promotional video
sections.wikitext: A promotional video for the song directed by [[Stanley Dorfman]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Humphries |first=Patrick |title=Top of the Pops: 50th Anniversary |publisher=New York: McNidder and Grace Limited |year=2013 |isbn=9780857160522 |edition=First |pages=3, 27 |language=English}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Simpson |first=Jeff |title=Top of the Pops: 1964-2002: It's still Number One! |date=2002 |publisher=BBC Consumer Publishing |isbn=978-0563534761 |pages=22 |language=English}}</ref> was filmed on October 19, 1964, in the rooftop garden of the [[Derry & Toms|Derry and Toms]] department store in [[Kensington]], London. The clip was filmed to air on ''[[Top of the Pops]]'' on October 22, as Orbison was unable to attend the show's live taping. It subsequently aired on October 29, November 12, and November 19.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

[[Van Halen]] recorded a cover of "Oh, Pretty Woman" to be released as a non-album single in January 1982 before a planned hiatus. However, the single's sudden success brought pressure from [[Warner Records|Warner Bros. Records]] to produce an entire LP; the resulting album, ''[[Diver Down]]'', was released that April.

On ''Diver Down'' and in the song's music video, "(Oh) Pretty Woman" is preceded by the instrumental "Intruder", which features frontman [[David Lee Roth]] playing an [[Electro-Harmonix]] synthesizer. Roth had written "Intruder" because the video the band had filmed for "(Oh) Pretty Woman" was longer than the song's running time.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2013-05-23 |title=Intruder |url=https://www.vhnd.com/diver-down/intruder/ |access-date=2023-02-17 |website=Van Halen News Desk |language=en-US}}</ref>

Van Halen recorded a cover of "Oh, Pretty Woman" to be released as a non-album single in January 1982 before a planned hiatus. However, the single's sudden success brought pressure from Warner Bros. Records to produce an entire LP; the resulting album, Diver Down, was released that April.

On Diver Down and in the song's music video, "(Oh) Pretty Woman" is preceded by the instrumental "Intruder", which features frontman David Lee Roth playing an Electro-Harmonix synthesizer. Roth had written "Intruder" because the video the band had filmed for "(Oh) Pretty Woman" was longer than the song's running time.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
{{more citations needed|section|date=August 2021}}
In the music video, filmed at [[Indian Dunes]] near [[Valencia, California]], the band members appear dressed as a samurai (bassist [[Michael Anthony (musician)|Michael Anthony]]), Tarzan (drummer [[Alex Van Halen]]), a cowboy (guitarist [[Eddie Van Halen]]), and [[Napoleon]] (Roth).<ref>{{cite magazine | url=https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/van-halen-best-music-videos-6568573/#! | title=Van Halen's 5 Best Music Videos | magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] }}</ref> Per a hunch-backed onlooker's request, they rescue a captive girl. It was one of the first videos banned by [[MTV]], due to its opening sequence featuring the captive girl (played by [[International Chrysis]]) being tied up and fondled against her will by a pair of [[Dwarfism|dwarves]]. At the end of the video, she is revealed to be a man cross-dressing. The ban was eventually lifted, as [[MTV Classic (American TV channel)|MTV Classic]] would later air the video.<ref name="Chad Childers">{{cite web |author=Chad Childers |date=7 December 2012 |title=Van Halen, 'Oh Pretty Woman' – Banned Music Videos |url=http://ultimateclassicrock.com/van-halen-oh-pretty-woman-banned-music-videos/ |access-date=March 21, 2015 |publisher=Ultimate Classic Rock}}</ref>

In the music video, filmed at Indian Dunes near Valencia, California, the band members appear dressed as a samurai (bassist Michael Anthony), Tarzan (drummer Alex Van Halen), a cowboy (guitarist Eddie Van Halen), and Napoleon (Roth). Per a hunch-backed onlooker's request, they rescue a captive girl. It was one of the first videos banned by MTV, due to its opening sequence featuring the captive girl (played by International Chrysis) being tied up and fondled against her will by a pair of dwarves. At the end of the video, she is revealed to be a man cross-dressing. The ban was eventually lifted, as MTV Classic would later air the video.

In 1964, the song was adapted into [[French language|French]] by [[Georges Aber]] as ''L'homme en noir'' ("The man in black") and performed by French pop singer [[Sylvie Vartan]] and backed by her brother [[Eddie Vartan|Eddie]]'s orchestra, released as a single in January 1965 as a non-album single. This version presents the "man in black" as a gunfighter who may or may not return to the woman who loves him. The single was backed by Aber's French adaption of "[[Can't You See That She's Mine]]" by [[the Dave Clark Five]], entitled ''N'oublie pas qu'il est à moi'' ("Don't forget he's mine").<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sylvie Vartan - N'oublie pas qu'il est à moi - ultratop.be |url=https://www.ultratop.be/fr/song/5dfdb/Sylvie-Vartan-N'oublie-pas-qu'il-est-a-moi |access-date=2024-06-20 |website=www.ultratop.be}}</ref> Vartan's version peaked at Number 15 on the [[Ultratop]] 50 charts in [[Wallonia]] in March 1965.<ref name="ultratop.be">{{Cite web |title=Sylvie Vartan - L'homme en noir - ultratop.be |url=https://www.ultratop.be/fr/song/9ad2/Sylvie-Vartan-L'homme-en-noir |access-date=2024-06-20 |website=www.ultratop.be}}</ref> Vartan had previously covered Orbison's "[[Dream Baby (How Long Must I Dream)|Dream Baby]]" in French as ''Cri de ma vie'' ("Cry of my life") on her 1962 debut album ''[[Sylvie (album)|Sylvie]]'', but it was not released as a single.

In 1964, the song was adapted into French by Georges Aber as L'homme en noir ("The man in black") and performed by French pop singer Sylvie Vartan and backed by her brother Eddie's orchestra, released as a single in January 1965 as a non-album single. This version presents the "man in black" as a gunfighter who may or may not return to the woman who loves him. The single was backed by Aber's French adaption of "Can't You See That She's Mine" by the Dave Clark Five, entitled N'oublie pas qu'il est à moi ("Don't forget he's mine"). Vartan's version peaked at Number 15 on the Ultratop 50 charts in Wallonia in March 1965. Vartan had previously covered Orbison's "Dream Baby" in French as Cri de ma vie ("Cry of my life") on her 1962 debut album Sylvie, but it was not released as a single.

sections.wikitext: During the UK leg of the [[American Heart World Tour]] in 2025, supporting act [[Elliot James Reay]] sang what was reported to be "a brilliant cover" of Pretty Woman, even though he and his band had only two days to rehearse the song before the first show in Belfast.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Campion |first=Gary |date=2025-10-24 |title=Benson Boone’s World Tour: A sea of sequins, moustaches & backflip after backflip! |url=https://www.gnimag.com/single-post/benson-boone-s-world-tour-a-sea-of-sequins-moustaches-backflip-after-backflip |access-date=2025-10-25 |website=gnimag |language=en}}</ref> Reay has repeatedly cited Orbison as a massive influence on his own work in interviews.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-13 |title=ELLIOT JAMES REAY: INTERVIEW |url=http://www.unclearmag.com/music-posts/2025/3/13/elliot-james-reay-interview |access-date=2025-10-25 |website=Unclear Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kuenzel |first=Antonia |date=2025-08-05 |title=Elliot James Reay Interview |url=https://principlemagazine.com/2025/08/05/elliot-james-reay/ |access-date=2025-10-25 |website=Principle Magazine |language=en-GB}}</ref>
